subsubtopic: BENEFITS TO WIDOWS AND CHILDREN OF VETERANS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the authority of Standing Order 43. Whereas more than 10,000 widows of deceased veterans and some 9,000 of their children were promised pension benefits over the next six years under Bill C-40, whereas many of these widows are left below the poverty line and may not survive until 1986 or 1987 and since the care of veterans and their widows and children is a national obligation and not just another piece of social legislation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker):
That this House request the government to find the money this year to pay these widows and children their proper pension benefits.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT CONSERVATIVE BUDGET PROPOSAL BE IMPLEMENTED-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, i rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Because of circumstances which menace and undermine the comfort and financial security of millions of Canadians living on low and fixed incomes, in view of the fact that since this government assumed office there have been six gas and home heating oil price increases, and that the government's action has added 20 cents per gallon at my home gas pump, not 18 cents, since December last, and because there is the threat of another 70 cents increase coming up, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid):
That the government act immediately to implement those provisions of the Crosbie budget which would bring energy tax credits-immediate softening tax relief-of $80 per adult and $30 per child which would have the effect of negating gas hikes for a family of four earning $21,380 or less annually and driving 20,000 miles per year, and also remove the tax on home heating oil which so adversely affects the 20 per cent of Canadians who can least afford it.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. It concerns a subject which I have raised with him in the House in the past, and this morning in committee, concerning the government's use of polls paid for by the people of Canada. Both in the past in the House and in the committee this morning the Prime Minister has indicated his willingness to have such information provided to the opposition and to the people of Canada. Regrettably, his ministers have not acted upon this principle.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister now if he will have the Minister of Justice table surveys on energy policy, which he said in the House on October 10 were to be used by the Liberal party in formulating its energy policy, as was revealed in the budget recently.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF ENERGY POLICY SURVEYS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot understand how the Leader of the New Democratic Party can say that ministers have not abided by this policy when just a few weeks ago the Minister of Justice made public the results of some 130 polls. There were some eight or ten exceptions to this, I cannot remember, but obviously the minister has abided by the policy which I stated.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF ENERGY POLICY SURVEYS
speechtext:

Well, the people have known for a long time that the Liberal government governs according to public opinion polls and surveys, but the issue at stake here is whether or not the people of Canada should finance them.

subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA-POPULATION ESTIMATES- EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS-PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Has the government of Quebec disputed the population estimates of Statistics Canada and, if so, what effect could such a difference of opinion have on equalization payments for the province?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of State, Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
subsubtopic: STATISTICS CANADA-POPULATION ESTIMATES- EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS-PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
The
Quebec government has made representations concerning use by the Department of Finance of official Statistics Canada population data for purposes of calculating provincial entitlements to fiscal equalization. The Statistics Canada population data used in calculating equalization are the June 1 census count for each province in a census year, and the most recent official estimates of provincial population as of June 1 for each year that is not a census year.
The government of Quebec has requested the Department of Finance to calculate equalization, commencing with the 198081 fiscal year, on a basis that would take account of the number of persons missed in the 1981 census. In every census, there are always people who are not enumerated. Statistics Canada has undertaken special surveys following recent censuses to estimate the number of persons missed. The survey made following the 1976 census was done on a province-byprovince basis. It indicated that the number of persons missed relative to the number counted was high in the province of Quebec. A similar survey will be made following the 1981 census.
Quebec has made representations that the population figures used in calculating equalization for 1981-82 should be based upon the official census count as of June 1, 1981, adjusted upward for each province to take account of the estimate of persons missed. They have also requested that comparable adjustments be made for years other than census years, commencing with 1980-81.
The effect on equalization of adjusting official population data for the number of persons missed in a census would be to increase entitlements in eligible provinces where the number of persons missed relative to the number of persons counted is high, and to reduce entitlements in eligible provinces where the number of persons missed relative to the number of persons counted is low. It is not possible to quantify such differences with respect to the 1981 census until the count has been tabulated, and the estimate of persons missed derived from the special survey that will follow that census. The results will not likely become available before October, 1982. Until that time, it will not be known whether Quebec would gain or lose, or by how much, from the methodology they have suggested.

Madam Speaker, after the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) has heard my remarks, it may well be that he will feel that all which needs to be said has been said with respect to the budget, and it will not be necessary for him to take up his ten or 20 minutes in the debate.
Just prior to orders of the day being called, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was over here. I asked him what he felt I should say about his budget, and he said, "Sine, say something nice". Frankly I have thought hard and long since he made that comment to think of something nice about the budget, and I think the House will understand when I say I cannot think of anything. If he had stayed a little longer with me, perhaps he could have made some suggestions.
As Hugh Anderson of The Globe and Mail said last weekend, the truth is that this budget may be a clever one but it is an exercise in the politics of wilful deceit. 1 say that because I feel the budget is not only deceitful, in its method of presentation, but I believe it is deceitful in that it is only half a budget. I suggest that perhaps this is the most significant matter which is being forgotten by members of the House and the public at large. We have heard only half the story from the Minister of Finance. In effect he presented what he feels, up to this stage, he can get away with, namely, an expenditure plan, an energy policy, the appearance that somehow taxes will not go up, and that is it.
Let me assure the House that the second boot will fall. It may take the form of another financial statement, it may take the form of some new budget, but the fact is that the figures
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
put before us if analysed, indicate only one thing, that a responsible government in this country cannot continue to allow the expenditure and revenue levels to continue as projected in the budget without the inevitable happening, that is, rampant inflation, rising interest rates, low productivity in industry, in short, utter chaos.
I say this in all sincerity. On behalf of Canada I ask, particularly those on the far left and on the rear left of the government benches, to come to their senses. They may be concerned about such things as the form, as to whether the constitution happens to be in this form or that form, but the time has come for the government of the day, on behalf of Canadians, to make some of the hard decisions and to put in place some of the measures needed to restore confidence in the country. Certainly that was not forthcoming in the budget brought in a week ago tonight.
It is truly odd that we in a country such as Canada must relive history which has been proven repeatedly to be wrong in other countries. I cannot understand that. The British tried this type of approach 20 years ago, this governmental intervention approach such as was displayed in the budget and the actions of the government. We know it did not work in Britain, and in fact they are in a massive reprivatization program in that country to try to right their economic ship. The people of that country were misled by the socialists in the Labour party. We in this country have been misled by the socialists in the NDP. Those pragmatists, those people on the government benches who say they will do anything if it means power, have let the country down by virtually introducing us to a socialistic state such as the one we in Canada are falling into.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The thing which disturbed me as much as anything since the return of Parliament has been to witness the absolute decline and eclipse of the Treasury Board as an effective arm of government in the present government of the country. I say that because we have known for some time that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is merely a token. In no way is he a man of restraint. He is a man with little clout within the cabinet ranks. He is simply filling a post with no say, but I never thought we would witness the day when a president of the treasury board would have the nerve- or perhaps he does not even know what he is saying-to walk into the House and make the statements he made yesterday. As reported at page 4362 of yesterday's Hansard, the minister said:
Unlike my predecessor, the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens), who kept trying to assume the responsibilities, in my judgment, of the Minister of Finance, I readily acknowledge the lead role of the Minister of Finance in developing the fiscal plan.
Near the conclusion of his remarks he referred to the Minister of Finance when he said:
All Canadians will welcome the frank and open way in which he has presented his expenditure plan and his medium-term economic assumptions.
What is the President of the Treasury Board saying? In effect he is saying that they have capitulated over at the

November 4, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
Treasury Board; they have surrendered. This was a fight which we waged with the big spending bureaucracy while we were in government. Essentially it boiled down to the simple fact that there were those who simply said, "You in the Treasury Board should do nothing but monitor. We at the lofty Privy Council level, overlapping the finance level and departmental levels, will come up with the expenditure plan which we think, in a macroeconomic sense, is needed in the country. You simply watch that the figures are spent the way we feel they should be spent." I know this may sound complicated, as if it is hard to understand, but let me assure the House that it is not.
There are two approaches to governmental expenditures. One is the academic approach, or the Keynesian approach, where those on high within the bureaucracy deem what a proper expenditure level is to be. Once that level is set, they simply sit down with those who might do the spending to figure out where it will be spent. I suggest that is what is now in vogue through the Michael Pitfields, through the lan Stewarts, through their respective ministers. In short, we do not have an expenditure plan in the sense that this is the least the government can spend. We have an expenditure plan which has been dictated by those who believe in big spending for the sake of big spending.
Here is the significance of what I am saying. Once this has been set and it becomes the fiscal plan, as the President of the Treasury Board says, or the expenditure plan, to use the words of the Minister of Finance, there is really no role for the Treasury Board. All the Treasury Board then does is add up the figures periodically and figure out whether they are under or over those expenditure levels which somebody else deemed are proper.
I have seen memos with respect to the previous government's handling of our affairs that indicate, for example, wastage is no longer to be criticized because wastage means simply that the expenditure plan, which is deemed to be proper, is perhaps not being met in the way it was originally intended, but at least it is getting the funds out there. That is what is going on. We are being told in the budget, which has been placed before us, that rather than spend $57.3 billion, as was our proposal in the Crosbie budget, that it is better to spend $59,350 million. Most important, we are being told that rather than spend $75,700 million by the fiscal year 1984, it is deemed better to spend $81,815 million.
Mr. Speaker, let me make one thing clear. I know it is commonplace for people to say, "Oh, well, he is simply trying to make a point but how does he substantiate it?" I invite hon. members, members of the press and the public, to take a look at a release that was put out by the Treasury Board on January 22, 1980. It is release No. 80-3. In that they will find we came up with figures comparing what would be the ongoing spending levels in government without the Crosbie budget, and what, in fact, those spending levels would be with the Crosbie budget. In short, we tried to translate to the public what the
ongoing expenditures in government were going to lead to if the Crosbie budget was not put in place.
I think what will be found to be most revealing now is that expenditure level is literally within millions of dollars each year-that is the ongoing trend line-it is literally within millions of dollars each year to what we were presented with Tuesday night here in the House of Commons. Thus, there is no restraint. All we have is rhetoric and verbiage on the part of that expert in verbiage, the Minister of Finance. What we have is the appearance of expenditures that are simply the trend line indicated by those who keep track of projections for ongoing programs and expenditures in government-no cutbacks. However, in contrast we had the courage through our budget to anticipate that those expenditures could be cut back by $7 billion by 1984. That was the approach that we took. We did not allow the ongoing trend line to take the Canadian public to a $82 billion expenditure level by 1984. We said that that was excessively high and must be reduced. We were able to propose that it be reduced by $7 billion.
Let me deal with the next point. So far I have simply been dealing with the figures that were brought into this House last Tuesday night by the Minister of Finance. But that is only the beginning. We find they have been doctoring the books. I understand the minister has an honorary degree, he is Dr. MacEachen. I did not realize that he got his doctor's degree for doctoring books. Let us take a look at a few of the examples. On page 32 of the budget papers you will find that it is revealed that they are setting up a new fund, if you like, called a petroleum compensation fund. Payments will be made out of that fund. The fund will be paid for this year in part, and in future years entirely, out of a petroleum compensation charge. Is it not interesting that in effect what they are doing-and after questioning the President of the Treasury Board last night he finally admitted that it was true-is giving the appearance of reducing expenditures by this little dodge alone to the tune of $1.2 billion this year, and up to over $6 billion by 1984.
Expressed in the simplest of language, what these artful dodgers are up to is simply that rather than follow normal accounting policies of this year, and saying they have to make payments with respect to oil compensation in the amount of $3,950 million, and record that in the blue book-while on the other side showing wherever they are going to get the revenue from-they have come up with a dodge, saying, "We are going to set up a separate fund which will be outside of the blue book. That fund is anticipated to need $3,950 million, but we anticipate we can sock it to the Canadian public to the tune of $1,215 million in the form of a new charge." That revenue will go directly into the fund leaving a net petroleum compensation payment of $2,735 million. And that is all that gets recorded in the accounts we have before us.
On that one item, Mr. Speaker, they have reduced the expenditure level by $1.2 billion in a most deceptive way. Taken through to 1984 we find that the total fudging of the books, if you like, will be $5.78 billion by 1984. With all sincerity I say that the Canadian public do not deserve that
November 4, 1980

type of treatment. How can you expect the Canadian public to have confidence in a government, or to have the proper attitude toward it, when government themselves are presenting figures in a way that, if you were in the private sector filing prospectuses with respect to share issues, you would literally be convicted of contravening the securities legislation on disclosure? That is only one example, Mr. Speaker.
I can add up totals of evasive types of presentations and non-disclosures totalling $10 billion by 1984. We have heard the Minister of Finance previously, and again today, come up with this figure of some $40 billion that he has saved the Canadian public. If he believes that, he is being fooled by his own fool figures. The fact is that the only reason he can pretend that he has saved anybody any money is simply that he is not disclosing it. He is simply not disclosing, to the tune of almost $16 billion in payment charges, the amount he is going to lift from the Canadian public in the charge for oil compensation to which I have been referring. For example his debt is another $13 billion higher in the aggregate than that proposed in the Crosbie budget. If you add those two things alone you have $29 billion of his so-called $40 billion saving. The reason I mention this type of thing is because I think it is so unfortunate that we have a Minister of Finance, in Canada's time of need, who stoops so low as to start cooking the books in that fashion.
Mr. Speaker, let me give you other examples of what I am referring to here. I say that there is $10 billion you can identify there by 1984 which would normally be considered expenditures, or amounts we have to allow for, that somehow or other they are shuffling off to the side-the Post Office approach. You will remember his cute little trick there. The Minister of Finance says, "Of course, I have assumed that the revenue from the Post Office will be sufficient to meet the expenditures and there will be no deficit during my projection." Expressed in another way, he is saying, "If we are able to roll onto the Canadian public directly the deficits of the Post Office through increased postage and other charges, then, lo and behold, we will have no deficit." He then has the nerve to say, "Of course, since we will have no deficit, and since I assume we will have no deficit, I will not show it in my figures."
There is the unemployment insurance dodge. What the minister is doing is taking it out of the general accounts, the estimates, and rolling it on to the employees and employers, and saying, "You will pick up another $1 billion between now and the end of the year", because it will allow him to show a more favourable budgetary presentation.

If we read between the lines, we must wonder what this budget will do to the agreements which now exist between the federal government and the provincial governments. The figures mean only one thing, that the government proposes to rewrite those agreements to put a greater load on
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
the provinces. There can be no doubt about that. That is another way the government will pick up what it thinks will be a $2 billion saving, and it will not be done in the federal name but simply picked up at the provincial level.
I mentioned these points because they show the mentality of the people who are now governing this country. Rather than face the hard realities, that expenditures are out of control and, that we need the strongest president of the treasury board possible, instead of a weak one, we are finding that the government is trying to disguise the figures. The government is in the lap of its public relations people who simply say, "It is perception that counts, not reality. Do whatever you have to do but do not tell the truth, and you will see how we will muddle through."
Let me put it another way. What we have received from the budget is an increase of 12.5 cents per gallon in the oil compensation charge, and an increase of 5 cents per gallon in the oil and gas revenue tax. Those figures total 17.5 cents per gallon, which compares to the 18-cent excise tax for which we were voted out. For half a cent on that item alone, the country changed from responsible government to irresponsible government.
As far as oil pricing is concerned, we are told that the increase will be $3.80 per barrel compared to our price of $4 a barrel. Of course, the 75 cents increase per barrel which the government ran up earlier in the year was not added to the $3.80 because it would put the price at over $4.50. The public relations people did not want to hear that on budget night so they said, "Let's forget that for the time being, and talk about $3.80." In truth that is what we have bought.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Deception.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Clearly, it is deception. In the words of Hugh Anderson, it is "wilful deceit" on the part of the government. The fact that the government has maintained the ongoing spending levels will have the effect of softening up and conditioning Canadian consumers to the concept that perhaps they should spend even more.
Last night the President of the Treasury Board startled myself and other members of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates by stating that he felt that 49 per cent of the people at the deputy minister's level in the public service were underpaid in this country. I do not know whether he based that comment on fact, or whether it was just a wish. But when the government is facing a deficit of $14 billion and serious doubts in the financial community as to whether the country can handle this debt load which the federal government proposes over the coming years, one of the last things it should be saying is that its employees, who presumably are partly responsible for the position which the government is in, should be paid more.
As a rule one pays for results. If the government were running at a surplus, or relatively close to a surplus, then 1 could see, if it were felt that somebody was underpaid, it as an opportunity to suggest a bonus or some other type of increase in pay. However, that is not the situation in this country today.

November 4, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Stevens
In short, we are in a very serious economic position which is not being dealt with in a prudent way by the government.
I mentioned my feeling that we have only received half a budget. The tax increases are yet to come, and let there be no doubt about that fact because it is just a question of form. What we have received so far is the energy aspect. I suggest that the reason energy has been singled out in the budget, and in the document entitled "The National Energy Program" is because the government feels that this field is an easy target. It looks upon the oil industry as predominantly foreign, as very profitable and as an industry which is mainly located in one province which represents only 10 per cent of the population of the country. In the thinking of this government, that industry is a fair target because it can arouse public opinion against that industry.
I hope that those people who read the budget and say, "Well, at least they didn't tax us too heavily," and those in industry who say, "Well, it's not hitting me, so somehow or other I am not concerned", do not smile too broadly, because I can assure them their time is coming should this government continue in office beyond its present mandate. The government intends to intervene, to socialize, to take over, to cannibalize, to Canadianize, to nationalize, call it what you want, until the Canadian public finally does what happened in Jamaica, Britain, and what will happen tomorrow in the United States, turn out the big spenders and bring in responsible government once again.
Approximately a week ago I attended a seminar in this city which dealt with public corporations. Various comments were made to rationalize the government's position on Crown corporations. The speaker just ahead of me made the comment that when the government wants to take over parts of the private sector, and the private sector resists because it does not want to be taken out, it should be remembered that the government has some very effective tools at its disposal. It can regulate the industry and it can bring in onerous taxation to sober it up. In short, the government can bring the industry to its knees so that it is willing to be bought out.
To show how much the government has accepted this theory, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) states at page 52 in "The National Energy Program":
The Government of Canada recognizes that the National Energy Program represents a fundamental departure, in many instances, from the current policy environment. Despite the fact that the policies will maintain, even enhance the relative position of the oil and gas industry, some firms may regard the new conditions as unsatisfactory. The government's acquisition program provides an answer for them. The Government of Canada is a willing buyer at fair and reasonable prices.
I thought that godfathers existed only in the United States, but clearly we have a godfather in the form of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Is that not contemptible? Did anyone ever think that in Canada we would reach the position where the government, which is supposed to be the servant of the people, rather than trying to respond to criticism would say, "If you don't like it we are going to buy you out on", presumably, "fair terms." I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that
with the power the government possesses, those terms would be virtually confiscation.
I mention this because I believe that if we in this House do not stand up and be counted, starting tonight, to show our distaste for this type of budgetary presentation, this type of spending, this type of deficit, this high infrastructure that will lead to greater unemployment in the country and unsatisfactory real growth in the economy, we will not have done our duty as representatives of our constituents.
I have spoken of some of the ways the government has deceived the people in this budget. Perhaps the worst deceit of all is the suggestion made during the election campaign that the government would control expenditures to the level of economic growth in the country. What is meant by that is not what you and I would mean, Mr. Speaker, that if the economy increases by 9 per cent this year we would try to keep spending down to 9 per cent instead of the 15 per cent the government project. The government means it will be kept to the-

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say how much I enjoyed the remarks made by the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens). It is nice that we are able to see the full epitome of the real Tory finally speaking up in this House. During question period we were treated to the exhibition of that sham Tory who shed great crocodile tears about the plight of the poor. He charged that this government was ignoring them and had not provided enough money in the budget to deal with the problems of those on low income. Now, however, we have the real voice of the Tory party speaking-no money for the poor-cut back-end the deficits. That is the pristine pure voice of the niggardly mean-minded sort of Tory who says, "No money for anybody; let's cut back."
1 enjoyed that, Mr. Speaker. I think it was useful to have that point of view expressed in this House-no more sham, no more charade, none of the posturing for the cameras. The hon. member has once again lived up to his reputation of being the true voice of the hard rockbed of Canadian Conservativism which holds, basically, that government should do nothing at all.
On this side of the House we appreciate all this, Mr. Speaker, because it shows what the differences are between us. I just wish, however, that the hon. member had been a little more accurate with some of the facts he put on record. I know that when he was a minister of the Crown he did not want to be confused by facts, but I would have thought that these past months in opposition would have changed his behaviour. Having occupied a cabinet post, I should have thought he
November 4, 1980

would have been more careful about what he presented as facts.
He said that he is tired of mythology and wants to get down to the real facts. Yet he was prepared to say in this House that the burden of unemployment insurance premiums was being hidden by this government, and he charged that this was an act of deception. What he failed to mention, however, was that the measure was introduced by his government in the December 13 budget-that the Crosbie budget introduced the principle that a greater share of the unemployment insurance program should be carried through the premium base. That budget recommended that the premium be increased to $1.60. When this government took office last winter, the premiums were frozen at $1.35 as it was felt it would have been awkward to continue with the plan of the previous government. Contributors were given a full year's respite.
It is a little unfair for the hon. member to suggest that the proposal to increase the unemployment insurance premium is an act of this government when, in fact, it was supported by members of his own caucus at the time the legislation was introduced. It was supported with a great deal of enthusiasm on the quite legitimate grounds that, over a period of time, the burden of the unemployment insurance fund had to be carried more equitably. The percentage of funds carried by the public sector had risen to 40 per cent, instead of the 20 per cent formula that the public sector had normally carried. We agreed the public sector was carrying a great burden. The hon. member forgot to mention, however, that his government introduced the measure and his caucus supported it.
While dealing with misstatements and errors or sins of omission, I think the hon. member would be the first to admit his own serious sin of omission. When dealing with oil pricing, he suggested that the formula we put forward included a Syncrude levy which would take it to above $4, and that the Tories would never have done that. We know that is not true, Mr. Speaker, because the Syncrude levy is a statutory requirement that every government would have to impose. Thus the Crosbie $4 increase would have become $4.75. In fairness, the former president of the treasury board should have acknowledged that.
If this debate is to be conducted with fairness, it would have been in the interest of honest observation and reporting for the hon. member to have been more accurate in the statements he made.
That brings me to the need for a more accurate and honest appraisal of the budget. Opposition spokesmen have raised cries of alarm up and down this country in the last week or so about the dastardly effect the budget will have on western Canada. Just this past weekend in my home city of Winnipeg, the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) suggested that this budget rang the death bell of federalism-that the Liberals will bring about separatism. Of course, he was prepared to say that he did not believe in separatism, but still most of his speech dealt with it. He implied that the budget discriminated against western Canadians.
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
The Premier of Alberta has suggested the budget discriminates against his province, that the government is moving into his living room to take over his furniture and all his services and resources.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) suggested that we would be embarked upon the slippery slopes of separatism if we follow the "made in Ottawa", central Canadian type of policy. Mr. Speaker, I am a western Canadian, and I do not think I take a backseat to anyone in this House when it comes to concern for my region and the type of development that should occur there. I take strong exception, however, to the fear tactics being parlayed by certain opposition spokesmen who suggest that there is a dichotomy-that the national government is not national at all but represents "them" and not "us". In a subtle manner they try to create a division in this country. They are employing the tactics of division for whatever cynical, political reasons they may have.
I know what the reasons are, Mr. Speaker.
As Minister of Employment and Immigration I will have to offer my services to the Leader of the Opposition within a few months. As an equal opportunity employer, the government is quite prepared to make sure that all the facilities of counselling and job placement are available to him when he needs them.
The tactics being employed by the opposition are very dangerous. They are playing with fire. They are taking the honest concerns and grievances that are felt in my region of the country, and in others, and fanning the flames into a conflagration, and then suggesting that there is a sweep of separatism emerging in the west when, in fact, the only separatism is in the minds of those who talk about it.
Sure, there are differences of opinion and there are honest criticisms about what we have done, but we are prepared to argue those criticisms and differences. However, we should not fall into the trap of this kind of fear-mongering which is simply trying to exploit those concerns and anxieties and turn them into something sour and distorted. That is mythology which is being parlayed in Canada at the present time is setting up a false distinction and a false dichotomy, trying to create divisions in Canada by employing the most exaggerated hyperbolic misstatements of facts that have ever been expressed in the history of this Parliament. We had some good examples in question period. We heard some absurd outlandish extrapolation of figures and ideas, which simply boggle the imagination until you know the people who expressed them, and then you understand why.
I am going to make a case this afternoon that the budget put forward last Tuesday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) does far more for western Canada, is far more in its best interests, than anything that was put forward by the previous government-those great paragons and defenders of the west. No matter how members on the other side try to cut it or try to divide it, when you compare those two documents, as members on the other side are fond of doing, and add up the

November 4, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
list of benefits that will accrue to western Canada, this budget comes out far more on the plus side than the one put forward by the former minister of finance and flabbergab last December 13. It is important that western Canadians understand that because western Canada will in large part be setting the agenda for discussion for debate over the next several years. It is the area where the dynamic growth in Canada will take place, and where much of the employment will occur, even though the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), in one of his flights of fancy this afternoon during question period, suggested that perhaps half of the province of Alberta was going to be unemployed. That was one of the most absurd statements that have ever been expressed in this House. It is in western Canada where the employment will continue to be.
I returned from western Canada last night. While I was there I met with representatives of the business community and the oil, gas and mining communities. Their concerns were not that of the member for Calgary West. Their concern was getting more people out to western Canada because they need skilled workers. Their concern was not the unemployment problem but to get more people from the other parts of Canada to work in the mines, the gas fields, and in natural gas exploration.
I would suggest it is about time the hon. member for Calgary West went home and talked to those people and understood what their concerns are, and not suggest something which is being manufactured or generated in his own very fertile imagination.

speechtext:
Let me indicate what the budget said. Let me point out, first and foremost, that we were responsive to the issues in western Canada by not putting in the budget many of the things being speculated about. There was a great sort of campaign being carried out. We heard such things as, "Look what these Liberals are going to do in western Canada. We will have an export tax". The battle flags were waving and the trenches were being dug purely on the idea of fighting this discriminatory tax. It was a legitimate concern to be raised, and one to which we responded by not bringing in an export tax. I am suggesting that we were prepared to respond to those concerns. We did not totally abdicate the need to get additional revenues for the federal government but we got those revenues in a different kind of way, through a different kind of mechanism.
Also introduced in that budget was a very clear strategy and program for ensuring that the major benefits of the revenues derived and developed out of the new resource boom of western Canada would be recycled back into the west. These revenues would be used for new energy supplies and sources,
for the industrialization of western Canada and to provide for conversion from oil to natural gas and electricity. These are energy sources in ample supply. So any suggestion that this budget ignores the concerns of the west simply means the provisions of this budget have been ignored.
The major beneficiaries of this budget-contrary to the point of view that was being put forward earlier in this House-are the consumers of western Canada and the consumers right across the country. A great deal of heartfelt anguish was being expressed on the part of some members about what was going to happen to the consumer. I will tell you what will happen to the consumers in my province. In 1984 they will be paying $400 to $500 a year less to heat their homes and drive their cars under this budget than under the previous Tory budget. That is the difference, Mr. Speaker. That is the real message of this budget. The Canadian consumer will find he is not paying the kind of inflated prices which were being put forward in the December 13 document of last year. It is that money which will stay in the hands of the consumer to buy other goods and services and which will keep the economy going.
Similarly, the farmers of western Canada will not have an excise tax on their fuel oil. They, too, are being saved by this budget. They will not have that kind of burden to carry which would add to their costs and, therefore, to the cost of food and agricultural products. That was avoided by this budget as compared to the document put forward by the so-called defenders of the west.
There are a series of major stimulants in the budget for the growth of industry in western Canada. I find it hard to understand why the Tories persist in assuming that the only agencies for the development of our energy fields must be multinational corporations. Why is it the Tories assume that it is impossible for Canadian-owned companies to become the major shareholders, the major entrepreneurs, the major enterprisers in the development of our oil and gas and our energy resources? What they are doing basically is defending the corporate system, instead of defending what should be the real opportunity, which is to develop new businesses in western Canada to provide for a whole new network of enterprise and activity through the incentive grant program. This is something that was not offered in the previous budget.
So, if we are comparing budgets and comparing measures, the opportunity for Canadian businessmen in western Canada to get an advantage and a step up in developing those resources, is in this budget. There are nothing of that kind in the previous one. It is out of that kind of incentive program, based around the idea that it is far more effective in our energy system to have Canadian-owned enterprises and companies, that we can avoid the massive transfusion of funds out of Canada which amounted to $3.5 billion in the past two years. That money could be kept in Canada working to develop new energy supplies and resources.

I think the hon. member for Calgary West has missed cheerleading practice, or something.
We are talking about a budget which is designed as a blueprint to encourage and develop western industry; to develop the very growth, jobs and opportunities that we think are so important to fuel growth throughout the rest of Canada. We should not be listening to the doomsayers and those preaching the gloom of depression and recession in the west, because this gives us an enormous opportunity, even for those companies I have talked about which are saying, "My goodness, we have had cutbacks and we have had our livelihood taken away from us". That is true, their percentage of revenues has been reduced, but the volume of money has doubled.
The amount of capital available to the oil and gas companies will double in the next three years compared to the last three years. There will be far more capital going in through private hands than there was up until last Thursday night. If hon. members opposite cannot read that in the budget, we suggest they take a Braille course because it is very clear that the full and necessary capital to provide for all the exploration and development is available.
Furthermore, we are prepared to take on this issue. We feel that that in itself is not enough. There must be more than that. There must be a very clear public role and responsibility in the development of our energy supplies. We make no apologies not only for maintaining Petro-Canada as an effective vehicle for energy development, but for enhancing its role. I will tell you one reason, as a westerner, because Petro-Canada is a western based company. It now provides jobs for over 2,000 people in the city of Calgary alone. It is a major sponsor of research and development, of new exploration and development projects right across Canada and in the international sphere.
As a western Canadian I take pride in the fact that this government was responsible for putting in place a brand new company which is now one of the major leaders and innovators in the energy field in the world.

subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What were our friends opposite doing? They were cannibalizing it. They were going to dismantle it. They were going to take it apart. Those great defenders of the west were going to subtract and eliminate one of the most important and effective agencies of energy development which this country has, a western agency of development.
To make the case further, I would point out it was just in the last week that we have taken the same model of Petro-Canada in the oil and gas field and applied it to the area of renewable energy and conservation technology. If members opposite ask what is in it for the west, 1 will say that in my own city of Winnipeg the new Enertech corporation is to be located. We have the opportunity of developing a brand new high technology there which will serve this country for the next 100 years. It is again a western Canadian city that will become
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
the centre of new skills, development, and innovation. It will put in place a brand new industrial base in western Canada.
Of course members opposite are going to vote against it because they do not believe in those kinds of things. They do not believe in enabling and assisting western Canadians to develop new technology, to develop new industries within their area, because they really are the friends of the multicorporations. That is their primary purpose. That is where their ambitions and concerns lie, not in developing Canadian companies, not with developing institutions that will be located in western Canada and will provide jobs and opportunities in the west. They are more interested in their friends in the boardrooms of Toronto. That is where their interest lies.
I will not accept this kind of mythology that is being expressed that somehow separatism will emerge because the west is being ignored. If there is anyone who has been guilty of ignoring the interests of western Canada, it is many of the members opposite who were prepared to support a budget last December that had nothing in it for western Canada, except a sell-out.
Further, we would like to point to the introduction in the budget of the western development fund. It is designed to take the proper profits and revenues deriving from resources and recycle them back into western Canada to provide a much more diversified economic base. There is not a westerner in this chamber who has not learned, as part of his history, the whole boom and bust cycle of the west based upon the erratic behaviour of commodity or resource markets.
One of the great ambitions of western Canadians has been to develop a broadly based economy with a wide variety of components of industry, processing and manufacturing, so that we can even out that boom and bust cycle and have a proper system of economic development which does not rely upon that uneven, bumpy road. That has been a ligitimate concern. It has not been met that well in the past.
I agree full well with all of the spokesmen from western Canada, provincial or not, who believe we should be using our resources and the revenues from them to provide for better economic development in western Canada. Where I take issue is with the way they chose to do it. Their choice is to leave all the control, responsibility and decision-making in the hands of individual provincial governments. They assume that will result in the kind of goal and ambition that we all share, which is the proper economic development of the west.
That flies in the face of the history of western Canada. Throughout the history of our region the federal government has always played an important and influential role in ensuring that the west world be developed. It was not the provincial governments which bailed out western farmers during the depression. It was the federal government that had to come to their rescue, based upon taxes drawn from other parts of the country.
It was the federal government which had to put the Wheat Board into place against the opposition of several provincial governments in order to provide for the orderly marketing of
onnnn ca

November 4, 1980
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
grain. When the issue of the 1940s and 1950s was the whole dry land farming problem, it was the federal government through the PFRA that came to the rescue of the prairies. It put in place the irrigation ditches and dug holes that provided proper watering resources for the west, oftentimes paid for by the tax dollars of Canadians from other parts of this country.
There is nothing wrong with that. That is what a federal government is for. It is to share the benefits and share the wealth. That is where we do take issue. That is where we divide, myself and those opposite, because we believe there is an important and necessary role for a central government to play in the development of western Canada, to its benefit and the benefit of the entire country. It is not to retreat and shrink our horizons, not to rely solely upon a provincial government because its own electoral mandate is only to serve the people within its narrow range of boundaries 400 miles wide. I would not expect them to do anything more.
I was a provincial member for seven or eight years. Your mandate is to serve a provincial constituency and jurisdiction. However, there is a fundamental difference when one becomes a member of the federal House and federal government. You realize there are choices that have to be made to serve one end of the country or the other.
It saddens me that so many spokesmen from the west are taking on that kind of parochialism. They say they do not care about the rest of Canada. They are not interested in sharing the wealth. They do not want to see a proper distribution of the benefits. They want to keep everything for themselves.
The fundamental flaw in that kind of reasoning is that, if we allow it to happen, not only does the west suffer in terms of its economic development, but so does the entire country. That is the central issue in this budget. That is where this budget differs fundamentally from the one we had on December 13. It does incorporate the basic idea of sharing and distribution.
The idea of the western fund is to use the federal jurisdiction which cuts across regional and provincial boundaries to put into place the kind of infrastructure that will help make the west grow. We from the west well know that one of the most serious concerns we have is in the area of transportation. We could be selling far more of our grain, potash, coal and other commodities, if we could move them to world markets.
The railways tell us that by this year their carrying capacity will be fully used, and in two years from now we will be 30 per cent short. We will all be losers if that takes place. Western Canada loses and so does the country. Therefore we must put in place a transportation program to modernize our entire distribution system for the western region. It must be not for one province, but for the entire region.
Who has the jurisdiction to do that? It is not the provincial governments but the federal government. The provincial governments are not in the business of trying to develop a full regional network of linking one part of the country with the other. That takes money. You do not wave a wand or snap your fingers and get the $6 billion, $7 billion or $8 billion it will take to modernize our railroad system in the west.
The money must be recycled. It must come from the fastest growing revenue source, which is the resource boom of western Canada. The benefits which flow out of that kind of investment are changing the tariffs, the rates and the Crow, and putting money into new tracks, terminals and ports. It means we all benefit from it. It is not a zero-sum game. It is not the "we" and "us" that the Leader of the Opposition was talking about on Saturday.
That is the kind of investment which will benefit all Canadians because, if we modernize our railroads, and the tracks are built in London, and the cars in Trenton, Nova Scotia, the entire country receives the full benefits of that kind of economic boom. That is what we are arguing about in this budget. The hon. member for York-Peel said that this is not a budget because it talks just about energy. No, we are not talking just about energy. We are talking about a fundamental question of how this country is going to be governed. Is it going to be governed in the interests of a few, or in the interests of the many? That is the difference, and that is the issue which is really joined in this Parliament.
